Dermatology · published research

Noninflammatory alopecia

In one seven-dog pilot, treated areas showed visible hair regrowth and substantially more hair-bearing follicles than untreated areas. This is a positive finding for that canine condition, but it has not been independently replicated or tested in people.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In one seven-dog pilot, treated areas showed visible hair regrowth and substantially more hair-bearing follicles than untreated areas. This is a positive finding for that canine condition, but it has not been independently replicated or tested in people.

Summary of the Evidence

One publication directly studies noninflammatory alopecia: a small within-animal controlled pilot in seven dogs with clinical and histopathologic confirmation. Each dog provided treated and untreated skin areas, and one dog also had tissue measurements. No independent replication or human study is identified in this category.

Human and clinical evidence

No human study was identified. The study concerns a canine alopecia phenotype and cannot establish an effect in human pattern hair loss, scarring alopecia, or other causes of hair loss.

Animal evidence

The treated skin areas showed visible regrowth in all seven dogs: six were described as having marked improvement and one as improved. The within-dog comparison is useful because treated and untreated areas belong to the same animal. In tissue from one dog, follicles occupied 18% of the treated sample area compared with 11% of the untreated area, and 93% of follicles in the treated sample were haired compared with 9% in the untreated sample. These measurements support the visible observation, but they come from one dog and should not be read as a group-level estimate (Olivieri et al. 2015).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate cell-culture or ex-vivo study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The canine protocol used three wavelengths together: 470-nm blue visible light, 685-nm red visible light, and 830-nm near-infrared light. The reported fluence was 3 J/cm², delivered twice weekly for up to two months. Because all three wavelengths were combined, the study cannot identify which wavelength contributed to the result. The protocol was tested only in dogs with the specified noninflammatory condition, not across other alopecia types or in humans.

Interpretation

The pilot found visible regrowth in all seven dogs and a large treated-versus-untreated difference in the follicle measurements available from one dog. That is a favorable result in the tested canine setting. A single small study cannot establish how often the response occurs, how long it lasts, or whether it applies to other animals or people.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term visible regrowth in the tested canine condition
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A seven-dog within-animal pilot reported visible improvement in every dog and large treated-versus-untreated differences in hair-bearing follicles. The internal comparison and tissue measurements strengthen the observation, but all evidence comes from one small canine study. Replication in a larger, clearly defined dog population and separate human studies would be needed before extending the finding to other alopecias or people.
